speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to advise that the governments of Canada and British Columbia have recently received from the Fraser river board copies of its report, "Final report of the Fraser river board on flood control and hydroelectric power in the Fraser river basin", and that the governments have agreed to release this report as a public document. I ask permission of the house to table the report of the board.
The plan presented by the board is designed to provide flood protection against a peak discharge from the natural basin of 600,000 cubic feet per second at Hope. The peak flow at Hope during the 1948 flood on the Fraser river was 536,000 cubic feet per second. The plan presented by the board would involve a cost of $4.9 million for dike improvements in the lower Fraser valley and approximately $400 million for diversion, power and regulating features in the upper basin. It would provide relief from flooding at Prince George, Quesnel, Kamloops, the lower Fraser valley and other points. It has been developed in a manner so as not to obstruct the migration path or affect the spawning grounds of any major salmon runs, and includes fish facilities to protect these runs.

I wonder if the Secretary of State for External Affairs is in a position to give a statement to the house regarding what is apparently a worsening of conditions on Cyprus following a decision by the United Nations a few days ago to provide a peace keeping force, and the failure up to this

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Martin (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: CYPRUS-POSSIBLE CANADIAN PARTICIPATION IN PEACE KEEPING FORCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity afforded by the question of the right hon. gentleman to say something further about the situation on Cyprus, which I know concerns all of us; in doing that, I should like to say that we all agree that Canada takes seriously its international responsibilities to the United Nations.
This applies no less to the situation in Cyprus than to the other peace keeping operations in which Canada has in the past, and is still participating in many disturbed areas of the world. We have repeatedly demonstrated our belief in international peace keeping operations as the only practicable method of dealing with regional disputes which have inherent in them the possibility of escalation into war. We believe in the fullest utilization of the machinery and techniques of the United Nations for this purpose.
These underlying principles have guided us in our consideration of the proposed United Nations operation in Cyprus to which, from the start, we have regarded ourselves, as the United Nations secretary general and the whole world would expect, as a responsible potential contributor.
I made clear yesterday that financing of the proposed operation, although a departure from past practice and from what is desirable, is not an obstacle to Canadian participation. Indeed, of the potential contributors Canada, apart from the United Kingdom, is the only nation to have been prepared to pay its own way as called for in the United Nations resolution and in default of a more appropriate arrangement.
I also made it clear yesterday that the duration of the assignment of the proposed force is no present obstacle. The resolution states three months, although that period would clearly have to be open to subsequent review in the light of the situation in Cyprus.
We recognized, when local and regional arrangements for order and stability in Cyprus began to break down, that the only way to preserve peace in the island was through recourse to the United Nations. And we have said so. We have been ready since that time

Inquiries of the Ministry to participate in a United Nations peace keeping operation, and have made military preparations which would permit us to do so quickly and efficiently. But we have also been aware that the force, when constituted, will be called upon to operate in ambiguous political circumstances, since there is no meeting of minds between the two communities within the island as to the meaning of the United Nations resolution adopted on March 4 this year, or of the purpose which the force it authorized is intended to fulfil. Moreover, the proposed force will face an operational situation in which it may face well armed and highly experienced guerilla forces. It is a situation in which there may be fighting.
It would have been irresponsible, as the government sees it, for us to have failed in our obligation to try to obtain in advance clearer understanding of the role of the force and reasonable assurance of the co-operation of the communities whose welfare they are being asked to protect. Our attitude has been welcomed by the secretary general, who acknowledges that we have been giving a responsible lead in ensuring that the United Nations operation is practicable and effective from the outset.
Difficulties of implementation of the security council decision have arisen because of the limitations which have been placed upon the United Nations ability to draw the force from all those nations willing and able to make an effective contribution. It has also been caused by failure to clarify the extent to which the two communities are prepared to co-operate with the force once established.
We have been pressing those most directly concerned to remove these obstacles to the creation of an urgently needed international force under the aegis of the United Nations. We are continuing to do so and we are ready to play our part the moment these difficulties have been overcome.
Only an hour ago I again conveyed these views to the secretary general of the United Nations, who reported to me on the nature of the progress that has been made in the negotiations that are under way with countries other than Canada which the secretary general would like to see participate in this force.
I can assure the right hon. gentleman that the situation in Cyprus, where order is being maintained by Her Majesty's forces from the United Kingdom, continues to engage our attention as well as that of certain countries in the United Nations which share our view as to the need for action in this matter.

Mr. Speaker, if I might preface this question, a number of letters have come to me in the last few days which enclose communications received by Canadians in all parts of our country from a certain group called the national white American party, the post office box number being given, asking for Canadian membership. These letters contain the most virulent and diabolical type of anti-Jewish propaganda and venomous attacks on the negroes of our country.

Mr. Speaker, as already appears from a few answers I have given this house, both the Department of Justice and the government are much concerned with the type of hate literature to which the right hon. gentleman has just referred. Not only the Minister of Justice but each minister of this government shares very thoroughly that concern.
With regard to the actual publication or the pamphlets which have been alluded to, this matter is presently being studied and looked into, with reference to which is the proper authority to assist in dealing with the matter, in the circumstances, once it has been fully investigated. However, a much broader question, as I have already said, is being raised, and it is that of ascertaining what would be the formula which could be devised and applied, which would be consistent both with proper respect of the individual, and of groups, as well as the respect of freedom of speech. As I see it, we must distinguish between the actual pamphlet under question, with regard to which I would not be free to give an opinion to the house at the moment, and second, the broader question as to what formula may be found.
I can only repeat that at four o'clock this afternoon I am meeting certain of the ethnic groups, that on Thursday I am meeting the Canadian Jewish Congress, and that both this house and those outside this house may be

I would like to begin today by recalling very briefly what has already taken place with respect to the very important constitutional obligation of readjusting the representation of the country in this house which falls upon parliament every ten years.
At the last session an act of parliament was put on the statute books and an appointment made in the statute itself of a representation commissioner who is to have the administrative responsibility for the new method of redistribution, for financing it under appropriations from parliament and for carrying on
Electoral Boundaries Commissions all the housekeeping. So we have already made provision for what I might call the administrative side of the task of redistribution, which is of course not at all the really important side but without which it cannot be effectively done in the new manner which all of us seemed to agree, in the debate we had at the last session of parliament, was desirable.
It will be recalled also, sir, that at the last session of parliament we had, both on the resolution preceding the representation commissioner bill and on the bill itself, not what I would call an extended debate but a pretty full debate in which the general principles were, I think, unanimously accepted by the house.
I would say there were two general principles that were accepted by the house. The first and by far the most important of these was that we should not follow the pattern that had been followed in the first 90 years since confederation, of having the readjustment of representation in this place done in this place by its members directly, but that it should be done by somebody which would be as impartial as we in our collective ingenuity could provide and who would be as competent as we could find means to provide through legislation and subsequent appointment. It was also agreed that in this process the government should have no more voice than any other part of the house, because this was a business which was peculiarly the business of parliament, of all of parliament, where we all have an equal obligation and, I hope and think, an equal desire to see that the people are fairly represented.
The second principle was that in doing this we should not abdicate the final responsibility which is imposed upon this parliament, and we would have to find some means of making sure that we did not just turn this matter over to a commission without any final power in parliament at least to object if any palpable and obvious errors seemed by the majority to have been made.
It is to achieve these two objectives that the bill now before us has been drafted. The previous bill was in a form quite similar to the bill that is now before us, but not precisely the same. The bill was introduced at the very end of last session. If I remember rightly, it was introduced on the last or the second last day of that session. There was an understanding at that time which the Leader of the Opposition expressed in a statement he made in the house on December 6, 1963 to which I should like to refer. He said:
We shall give every co-operation in the passage of the legislation setting up the representation commissioner-

Electoral Boundaries Commissions
I acknowledge that every co-operation was given in all quarters of the house:
-of course, during the recess we shall be able to meet with representatives of the government and of other groups in the house to discuss this important matter of redistribution legislation.
It was not actually possible to have any such meeting during the recess, but in the opening days of the session, thanks to the co-operation of the representatives of all groups opposite, we did have a certain measure of conference and consultation. In that conference and consultation I made it very clear at the beginning that no one had committed anyone else at that meeting; that it was just for the purpose of trying to find out as far as possible what we all thought would be acceptable and putting that into the bill, so that the matters we would have to debate when the bill came before us would be those on which there were understandable differences of opinion.
It is not for me to say whether we achieved that purpose. All I can say is that I thank all hon. members on both sides of the house who took part in those consultations, and I want to make it very clear that they bound no one to anything at all and that every hon. member is perfectly free, so far as I am concerned at any rate, to express his views on this matter. There will be no allusion whatsoever in the debate to any of those discussions.

that was a matter of difference in our debates before the prorogation of the last parliament-that there shall be a separate commission for each province. I am frank to admit that this is a matter on which there is not- certainly so far as I know-agreement in the whole house. But I want to explain very briefly why my colleagues and I came to the conclusion that we should at least put the bill forward in that form at this time for the consideration of the house. I think it was made abundantly clear to me, and I think to my colleagues, that it would not be possible within the life of this parliament to have a single commission for the whole country carrying out the necessary work in the time that would be available, to make sure that in this parliament we did perform the constitutional function that we are called upon to perform. Because the amount of physical work which would be required in the delimitation by any commission, however diligent, raises a problem here.

speechtext:
I am seeking to follow a certain line of argument here, so would the hon. member save his question until the end?
With regard to the personnel of commissions, I should like to say parenthetically that there is a real problem in getting people who will not only be fair but who will appear to everyone to be fair. Also I do not think there will be any disagreement that it is going to be essential to get people who occupy eminent positions in the community. People who occupy eminent positions in the community are people who, in general, have other duties to perform in the community in addition to the duties they would have as commissioners, and to get men or women of sufficient eminence who would be able to devote their full time to this task over the period which would be necessary to effect redistribution for the whole country would, I think, be an impossible task.
I think if it were not for the time factor I would agree with what several hon. gentlemen, including the right hon. Leader of the Opposition, said in earlier debates, that ideally it would be preferable if one commission could do it for the whole country. In that event you would be quite sure that they would follow precisely the same criteria throughout. But once we became convinced that that would be virtually impossible within the probable life of a parliament, the next idea which occurred to those of us who were working on the matter was that we might have four commissions. It was quite clear that the two provinces which presented the largest problems and which would take the

largest amount of time were the provinces of Quebec and Ontario, and that the time which would be required for the delimitation of the constituencies of the other provinces would obviously be much shorter if there were the same diligence and competence applied to the problem. It did seem that perhaps if we had one commission for the four eastern provinces, one commission for the four western provinces, one for Ontario and one for Quebec, that might be sufficient.
Then when we began to think of what that would mean, unless it was a very large commission there would probably be only one person on the commission from each of those provinces. There would only be one person from each province who would be apt to have that kind of local and particular knowledge, such as geographical knowledge, knowledge of the history of the province, topographical knowledge, and knowledge of other matters which are really essential to do this job properly, and as a result it would be unlikely that there would be agreement to just one person from each province.
I must say that I myself reached the conclusion that the only answer to this problem which was feasible and practical was to have a separate commission for each province. Obviously in the case of some of the smaller provinces the commission might not take very long to do its work; but if it did not take very long to do its work it would be correspondingly less costly, and therefore, from the point of view of economy or anything of that nature, nothing would be lost by having one commission for each province.
I must confess that when I came to this conclusion in my mind I had not yet heard the report that Mr. Castonguay brought back from Australia. After his return from that country he told me that the same question had arisen there at the very beginning but that it had been discarded, he did not know for what reason. In Australia they had always had one commission for each state for the federal redistribution, and it seemed to me that because the experience in Australia had on the whole, I think, been a very satisfactory one-there has been very little political or partisan controversy about the results of their redistributions-it seemed powerfully to reinforce in my mind the impression that I had reached. It is for that reason that the proposal to set up 10 commissions has been left in the bill.
Next we came to the very difficult problem of determining the composition of the commissions. I think I expressed the view, which I think the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre also expressed, although I am speaking from memory and if I am wrong I should like to be corrected, that the experience in 20220-48
Electoral Boundaries Commissions Manitoba with redistribution had been very satisfactory. In Manitoba the chief justice of the province, the president of the university and the chief electoral officer were designated in the legislation by office and not as persons. This produced a commission that commanded universal respect and confidence, and whose report was, I think, only altered with respect to one or two names. In every other respect it proved very satisfactory.
I must say that a good many of us racked our brains to see whether we could find people who, first, this parliament would have the right to designate. It is one thing for the provincial legislature to say that the chief electoral officer of the province should do something, but he is an officer of the province. We might achieve the same thing by getting their consent to it, but the parliament of Canada could not impose that duty upon him by naming his office; at least I would think it would be a very dubious proceeding to try.
However, I do not think that at all rules out the possibility that with the consent of a provincial government the person who occupies the position of chief electoral officer might serve, and serve very acceptably, on one of these commissions, or as far as that is concerned on all of them. But quite frankly, apart from the chief justice of the province or a judge designated by the chief justice of the province-and here I must say I was very much influenced, as I think were others too, by the Manitoba precedent-it did not seem to us that there were any other persons we could designate who would have the same title and position in all provinces. In any event, what we really wanted was to be assured of impartiality.
After various other possibilities were considered the government finally agreed to put in the bill the suggestion that the chief justice of the province should nominate the chairman from a member of his court; that the leader of the government, the Prime Minister, should nominate one of the members of the commission; and that the Leader of the Opposition, who is an officer of parliament, should nominate the other. I say unreservedly that I have every confidence that no matter who occupies those offices, any person who becomes leader of the opposition in the parliament of our country or prime minister in the parliament of our country would take this responsibility seriously and make the kind of nominations that all of us would feel were appropriate under the circumstances. I do not hesitate to say that with respect to this provision or with respect to any other method which commends itself to the house or to a majority

Electoral Boundaries Commissions of the house and which seems likely to produce as fair and effective a result, the government will be quite prepared in committee to consider on its merits any amendments to this procedure.
The fourth member of each commission, and I think this met with general approval in our debates last session, would be the representation commissioner himself. The reason for making this suggestion is that he would be able by being there, not only to provide the tremendous technical knowledge that we all know the particular representation commissioner we now have possesses, but also by his presence on all the commissions he would go a long way toward assuring that similar methods, similar techniques and similar criteria would be used by the commissions in performing their functions.
Frankly, sir, up to now this is the most satisfactory suggestion we have been able to think of for arriving at the composition of these commissions, but I hasten to say again that if anyone in any quarter of the house can produce a better method we have an open mind. It is, I say once more, not the special responsibility of the government but the responsibility of all of us to do this in the best possible way.
We come then to the next question, the preparation of the reports. It will be noted that the most important aspect of the preparation of the reports is not, of course, the basic question of how many members each province shall have, which is determined by the British North America Act as amended, but how the constituencies within each province shall be divided. The method is a very simple one. Basically I think it is perhaps the only possible method. It is exactly the same method suggested in the bill introduced by the right hon. gentleman in another parliament although the details are not the same. It is that the population of a whole province be divided by the number of members to arrive at a quotient which should be the basic, standard representation for each constituency, and that the commission should have a certain tolerance above and below that quotient.
I think it was clear from the debates we had before prorogation that this is the point on which undoubtedly the sharpest differences are likely to occur in the house. We recognize that. The government for its part has suggested that the tolerance should be 20 per cent each way; in other words, that a constituency might have one fifth more than the suggested number of residents or one fifth less. This represents, of course, quite a large number of people.
At the same time I recognize as much as any member of the house, I think, that there
[Mr. Pickersgill.l
are geographical peculiarities about our country, that the northern constituencies in nearly all the provinces have huge areas, that they do present special problems and that it may be felt by a majority of the house that a 20 per cent tolerance is not large enough.
I doubt that we would have any strong argument that it is too large, though it is interesting to note that in Australia it has been proposed for quite a long time, though actual legislation has never been put on the statute books, that the tolerance be cut to 10 per cent, and in New Zealand it is only 5 per cent. But I do think particularly at this time, having regard to the fact that this is the first redistribution to be carried out under this system, that 20 per cent is the lowest tolerance I would be prepared to recommend.

I also suggest that there should be one commission rather than 10. Clause 5 of the bill introduced by the former government sets forth the composition of the commission, and states:
The commission... shall consist of five members one of whom shall be the person for the time being holding the office of chief electoral officer of Canada and the remainder of whom shall be named in the proclamation establishing the commission.
I should now like to refer to the last section of the same bill introduced by the former government, clause 20, which reads as follows:
The governor in council may make regulations, generally, for carrying into effect the purposes and provisions of this act.
Clause 16 of this present bill provides that a commission which is set up-
-may make rules for regulating its proceedings and for the conduct of its business, and may provide therein for the conduct of any inquiry or hearing by one or more of its members.
That means that there is the power in each one of these commissions to make its own rules and regulations, and we might wind up with having as many different sets of rules and regulations governing the conduct of each commission as we have commissions, which seems to me to be one of the more serious defects in this legislation.
This opinion is shared by the editor of the Edmonton Journal who on December 2, 1963 set forth his criticisms in an article, to which I should now like to refer:
The federal government is proposing ten commissions, one for each province, to work out the redistribution of parliamentary seats. How can such a system expedite the task and serve better than a single commission?
The difficult and time-consuming parts of the job would be the working out of an acceptable formula for redistribution and the settlement of the vexing questions of equitable application among provinces and regions of the country.
Those are the rocks on which redistribution, when not frankly a gerrymander, is most likely to founder. Ten commissions will have far less chance of avoiding the shoals than one. And even if they should scrape by, they would almost certainly take longer than a single compact body to chart a common course on paper and to agree finally on how to sail the flotilla, intact, into harbour.

Electoral Boundaries Commissions
It is not difficult to imagine the ten sailing away in different directions and having a bitter time reassembling near the end of the voyage. Mr. Nelson Castonguay, the chief electoral officer, would have an unenviable task as co-ordinator-in-chief, shore-based at Ottawa.
I know the minister is a nautical man so perhaps he has a certain amount of sympathy with the tenor of this editorial, which concludes as follows:
Why not make him operational commander of a single commission and divide up the work among the members as necessity demands? That is close to what the opposition advocates and it looks like a much more promising procedure.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that by duplicating commissions it will only have the result of duplication of effort. I realize the argument is that a commission in each of the provinces will be more familiar with local conditions, but at the same time the overwhelming argument is to get the work done as quickly and as efficiently as possible. I think ordinary principles of management might dictate that one commission would serve much more effectively than ten. There is also the problem of 10 different sets of rules; there would be no assurance whatsoever that the commissions would come up with a uniform set of rules and regulations governing their procedures and hearings even though there was the co-ordinating influence of Mr. Castonguay on each one of the commissions. It is more probably the case that you would likely have 10 disunified commissions. Therefore, this is another argument for a single commission.
Another argument lies here. The legislation stipulates that the chairman of each commission has to be the chief justice of the province-I think that is the phrase used. According to clause 6 it is provided that:
The chairman of the commission for a province shall be appointed by the chief justice of the province from among the judges of the court over which he presides-
I realize that the minister is not a lawyer, but there is some doubt existing in some provinces as to who is the chief justice of the province. Recently there was a case in the province of Saskatchewan in which doubt was expressed as to whether the chief justice was the chief justice of the court of Queen's bench or the chief justice of the court of appeal. Which chief justice does the legislation mean here? I see the minister is laughing at my remarks, but I am quite serious when I say this; and there is a case on the law books of this country which will disclose, if the minister cares to get his advisers to look at it, that there is some very serious doubt in this regard.

He said: Mr. Speaker, my purpose in moving second reading of this bill is not so much that I consider the matter of the right of Indian people to consume liquor to be one of overwhelming importance but rather that I consider the principle involved in the bill a most important one. I feel that the passage of the bill will serve as evidence to the Indian people of our good faith, and indicate that we in this parliament are willing to take definite steps toward the restoration to these people of the rights which over the years and, indeed, over the centuries we have gradually taken away from them.
Hon. members will recall that a bill in identical form was moved during the last session of the house, and its purpose is quite simply stated. It will remove from the Indian Act the discriminatory features which make it possible, and I think one might go so far as to say encourage, provincial jurisdictions to deny to the Indian people the same rights in respect of liquor laws that are possessed by the remainder of the residents of the provinces. The bill is on all fours with the recommendation of the joint committee on Indian affairs which made its second and final report to the House of Commons on July 8, 1961. No action has been taken by either government since that time to implement the recommendations of this committee.
In my opinion it is high time that we made some progress in implementing the recommendations of that committee, recommendations which many of the Indian people of this country felt were almost as good as law once the report of that committee had been accepted by the house. In my view we have been moving very slowly in this field as well as in the general field of the restoration of the rights of the Indian people. As far as action in the house is concerned, we have fallen far behind the considered opinion of people who are expert in this field.
To illustrate my contention I should like to refer briefly to the report submitted to the government and the legislature of the province of Manitoba by the social and economic research office of the department of

agriculture and immigration of that province. The report is a study of the population of Indian ancestry living in Manitoba and, as I say, the study was undertaken by the social and economic research office under the direction of Jean H. Lagasse who was director of the research office at that time. The report was made in the year 1959, some two years prior to the report of the joint committee of the house and the other place on Indian affairs. I wish to refer to page 165 of volume 1 of the report where there is a quotation from an earlier report on an investigation in 1955 by the Manitoba liquor inquiry commission under the chairmanship, I understand, of Mr. John Bracken. In their report that commission had this to say:
It is our view that while Indians have many problems arising from the use of liquor, that so long as they continue to be wards of the state and denied privileges others receive and are thus forced to buy liquor illegally at double the ordinary price, and to consume it in circumstances far from respectable, that the present unsatisfactory conditions will continue.
There we have the considered opinion of the Manitoba liquor inquiry commission as long ago as 1955. The report of the Manitoba social and economic research office goes on to say that conclusions similar to those reached by the Bracken inquiry were reached by the Hawthorne study of Indians in the province of British Columbia. In fact, the report states:
Similar conclusions were reached by Hawthorne in his study of the Indians in British Columbia. Federal authorities could be approached, with a view to working out a method for placing the Indians under the same liquor legislation as other Manitobans.
As I mentioned earlier, the Bracken report was made to the government of Manitoba in 1955. Yet it will be recalled by some hon. members that in 1956, even after studies of that kind had been initiated and were under way, the discriminatory provision which I seek to remove by my bill was put in the Indian Act at that time, the last time that the Indian Act was amended in this regard. The general effect of the 1956 amendment was, shall we say, to liberalize the opportunities of Indians to enjoy their rights as citizens in this connection, but the discriminatory provision which gave the provinces the option of deciding whether the Indian people could enjoy the same rights as provided under the laws of the provinces for other citizens was retained in the Indian Act.
So I feel there should be little argument or discussion about the immediate passage of this bill by the house. I realize this is only a small segment of the action which should be taken by the house in connection with the affairs of the Indian people. It is a perfectly simple, straightforward proposition. It will implement a recommendation in almost the exact terms
Indian Act
which was adopted by the house in an earlier parliament. Therefore, as at least an indication of our desire to move forward more rapidly than we have been in restoring to the Indian people their rights and privileges, I believe that the least we can do at this time is to pass this bill.
I should point out that the bill I am presenting preserves the right of the Indian people to decide for themselves whether or not they wish to have liquor upon their reserves. The present provisions, which provide for a plebiscite, are carried forward. The bill simply consolidates those sections of the Indian Act which have to do with the whole matter of the use of liquor by Indians. It eliminates the superfluous sections and sets out a simple, straightforward proposition that the Indians in any part of Canada will enjoy the same rights and privileges as other residents of Canada in respect of making a private decision as to whether or not they shall partake of spirituous liquors in any way, shape or form.
I hope, therefore, that the house will be prepared to give second reading to this bill at this time in order that we can go into committee of the whole to consider the matter. I feel quite certain that if there should be any minor, technical objections to the phrasing of the bill, we can very quickly straighten them out in committee. I am not interested in every comma that may be in the bill, but I do feel we could proceed at this time to approve of the bill and perhaps deal with it expeditiously in committee.

Mr. Speaker, I only rise to take part in this debate for a very few minutes. In doing so, I should like to express the feeling that the problem of liquor, while not confined to Indians by any means, is a very grave problem indeed. This question of liquor for the Indians has many ramifications, the results of which are not very good in some cases. We all agree that there has to be a time when the Indian population will take upon themselves the responsibilities and privileges which are accorded to all citizens.
However, there is a great deal of difference in the capacity of individuals to consume spirituous liquor. This individual capacity has created a far reaching problem so far as the Indian population is concerned. I do not believe there is anyone who could be more concerned with this problem than those individuals who live close to Indian populations and have had the opportunity of assessing the influence of liquor upon them. It is a heart rending sight to see these people, who are just as much human beings as we are and have all the rights and privileges we have, with black eyes and torn clothes emerging from alleys. It is true that there are

Indian Act
a good many white people in some of these districts who do the same thing, but many of these white people have had an opportunity to consider this whole problem. The criticisms that may be made of a white person should not be made of an Indian in many cases. As I say, we are hoping that the time will come when the Indian population is able to take on the responsibility it should have.
We must be careful, however, in anything we do in this House of Commons to ensure that there is not a continuation of the buckpassing we have seen in connection with Indian affairs between the provincial and federal jurisdictions. In many cases, no one seems to be able to define exactly whose responsibility it is to do certain things on behalf of the Indian population. We are aware also of the fact that many of the Indian bands are not in accord with the idea of having liquor on their reserves at all. This is covered by the fact that there is a provision for local option. I do not think the cost to the province, so far as liquor for Indians is concerned, is any greater than it is so far as whites are concerned. I think there is more destruction and mischief in this connection so far as the whites are concerned. If this is true, then I believe that the provincial governments concerned, or any other jurisdictions concerned, should be prepared to spend more money and more time in getting expert advice and counsel in connection with this problem. I believe that one of the things that has to come, and the sooner the better, is a complete clarification of the situation of the Indian population in respect of their citizenship. As has been pointed out, there are many situations in which the Indians are given the feeling they are second class citizens. I am in favour of eliminating this situation at the earliest opportunity.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING POSSESSION AND CONSUMPTION OF INTOXICANTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak on this subject not only because it is a question that comes under the jurisdiction of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration but because in my constituency, almost within the city limits of Fort William, there is an Indian reserve where I have many friends whose friendship I cherish. These Indians are wonderful people, quite capable of integrating into our white way of life. Some of them are still suffering from a low economic standard because they have inadequate training. Some of the younger generation are taking advantage of the educational facilities available, and I expect that within a few short years their standard of living will rise to the level of that which is now enjoyed by the average citizen of our country.

The bill under discussion is similar to Bills Nos. C-26 and C-124 introduced by the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) on January 22, 1963 and September 11, 1961, respectively. It is identical to Bill No. C-34 introduced by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett), which was debated on December 6, 1963. The principle of the bill, Mr. Speaker, is quite acceptable in that it proposes to do substantially what we have included in our own preliminary draft amendments to the Indian Act. The bill, in effect, repeals the liquor provisions of the Indian Act, sections 93 to 96A, and substitutes provisions which would make it an offence to sell, give, possess or manufacture liquor on an Indian reserve, subject to local option with respect to possession.
Amendments to the Indian Act will be proposed at the appropriate time. The liquor provisions will be considered then.
It is not a question, however, of the Indians not being able to obtain liquor privileges. The act as it now stands provides the means. The question is whether it is desirable to proceed with a separate bill dealing only with the liquor provisions.
The reason for this has to do in part with the need to consult with the Indians on the proposed legislation. It is the firm policy of the government to consult Indians on matters of importance to them in the legislative field. In view of their interest and, it may be added, their divergent views as expressed in the past on the subject of liquor, they ought to be given an opportunity to make their wishes known.
There is no question of urgency about passing Bill No. C-6. The privileges proposed by the bill are already available to Indians where the provinces of which they are residents are prepared to grant them. The Indian Act now provides for a gradual assumption of privileges. In the first place, under section 95 partial privileges may be given; that is, the right to purchase and consume intoxicants in public drinking places. This right has been granted in British Columbia, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Ontario, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Yukon and Northwest Territories.
Indians may also purchase and use liquor off their reserves in the same manner as other residents in Ontario, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, New Brunswick, Yukon and the Northwest Territories. In these provinces, therefore, the Indians may either drink in public drinking places or in any home or place off a reserve.
Finally, in some of the provinces Indians may, on a local option basis, have liquor on their reserves. As a matter of fact there are many reserves where this privilege has already been granted, such as British Columbia,

55 bands; Saskatchewan, 13 bands; Manitoba, nine bands; Ontario, 42 bands; New Brunswick, five bands, and Nova Scotia, three bands. It is clear that the Indians may, and have in fact, been receiving liquor privileges since the Indian Act made provision for this for the first time in 1951. The way is open, therefore, through appropriate action of the provincial authorities and/or the band councils, and concurrence of the governor in council, for liquor privileges to be extended to the extent of that contemplated in Bill No. C-6.
The only provinces where liquor privileges to Indians have not been available are Alberta, Quebec and Prince Edward Island. As far as is known there has not been any strong agitation on the part of the Indian people of these provinces to have the privileges extended to them.
I am an ardent advocate of lifting the standard of living of our first citizens, by every means available. Opportunities must be provided for opportunities for employment, in mines, in fisheries, on farms, in industry and in city jobs.
Senator David Croll, speaking to a meeting of the Catholic charities council a year or so ago, suggested that the Indians should have direct representation in the House of Commons. This suggestion would cut across tribal lines and give them a sense of participation in Canadian affairs. I submit that one or more constituencies could be created with an elected member from each. This is one sure way of bringing the Indian people into the Canadian stream of life quicker than by any other method.
Indian Act
Anyone who has lived or worked with Indians must admit that they have a fine sense of humour and spend much time laughing over the incongruities of our ways of life and how we make choices which they think are so stupid.
They are very observant people because they enjoyed a hunting and fishing culture such a short time ago. Keenness of observation in this culture was the difference between life and death in the battle with the elements and the animal world for food. They notice things about people that we do not even suspect.
They have a mixture of their own culture and what they have accepted from the newcomers to their land. It is a changing and growing culture, we might call it the adolescent part of society which has evolved lately in Canada and, like all adolescents, they are rebellious and not certain of what they want. They are a proud people and wish to preserve their cultural identity but they do not fully realize the price they are paying for this and will have to pay in the future to preserve this status.
Their native intelligence is equal if not better than the rest of Canadians but for lack of educational facilities and lack of motivation for formal education, they impress teachers as being a dull lot with very few outstanding students. This is unfortunate because it does not give a true picture of the Indian's ability. This can only be changed by time and effort.
I was a member of the joint parliamentary committee on Indian affairs during the 1958, 1959, 1960 and 1961 sessions of parliament,' and in all the submissions presented to the committee by several bands from coast to coast, none of them made requests for liquor rights in reserves. Their primary concern was with schools, health facilities, timber cutting rights, fishing and hunting rights and better housing.
It seems to me that there is no urgency in the question contained in this bill.
I have great faith in this government. I have confidence in the good intentions and good will of the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, to bring about legislation which will bridge the gap between the old and the new way of life for Indians everywhere in Canada.
Lest I should be misunderstood, I wish to make it clear that I am not advocating the compulsory abolition of the reserve system as such. I think the Indians themselves would strongly oppose being all of a sudden deprived of their reserves. What I am advocating is a system which would improve the lot of the Indians by education and job opportunities, by developing their agricultural and reforestation potentials within their own reserves, such as those in the Thunder bay, Kapuskasing and Cochrane areas in northern Ontario.
Reverend Father Mulvihill, a missioner who lived for 20 years in Indian reserves and who has great practical experience of Indian education in British Columbia, not long ago wrote a pamphlet, and I wish to quote a few paragraphs from it:
m the memorandum of the joint parliamentary committee on Indian affairs in 1961, a reference was made to the question of liquor, and I wish to quote two short paragraphs from it:
It is suggested that serious consideration be given to removing the liquor provisions of the Indian Act with the possible exception of local Indian option for on-reserve possession. This would place basic responsibility respecting the use of intoxicants by Indians at the provincial level where it now rests in so far as use by other citizens is concerned.
With regard to the retention of local Indian option for on-reserve possession, it is envisaged that referendums would be held at the request of the band council. Such a provision would to a degree keep Indians in a separate category. On the other hand, since possession of intoxicants on a reserve would be a matter of choice by the Indians, the Indian Act could not be regarded as arbitrary in this respect.
So it will be seen that this question was considered at the time when this particular parliamentary committee heard so many submissions from Indians all over the country.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Tremblay) has indicated to me that it is his purpose to

Indian Act
follow the forward looking Liberal policy in dealing with Indians which was promised by his distinguished predecessor, the present Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau). This government has every intention of extending to the first citizens of this country every consideration in matters of education, housing and employment.
A few days ago the minister announced that a conference with the provinces would be held in May for the specific purpose of discussing Indian affairs to enable the Indian people to gain equal access to social and economic welfare with other Canadians. Presently before the United States congress is bill number HR-980 called the civil rights bill for Indians. This measure calls attention to the civil rights of Indians and mentions the Indians as being a forgotten race; while everyone pays lip service to the fact that the white man owes a great debt to the Indian people, little is being done, notwithstanding.
I am confident that this government will tackle the problem by extending job opportunities to them in every way possible. In short, I have every reason to believe that it is the present government's intention to greatly strengthen the administration of the Indian affairs branch and encourage participation of trained and educated Indians in carrying out the program to promote the welfare and to improve the opportunities of Indians, so that they can share to the full in the life of their country.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING POSSESSION AND CONSUMPTION OF INTOXICANTS
speechtext:
I am not too well prepared to participate in this debate, but I feel I want to say something in support of the bill as moved by the hon. member promoting it.
I feel I can support this bill only on the basis of the principle that we must not categorize people. When we find different pieces of legislation aimed at different groups of individuals I seem to want to be against them. If there is really no other way of helping Indians with their liquor problem, and it certainly is a problem, my statement in support amendment or liberalization of liquor laws for Indians does not take away from my acknowledgement of the fact that this is a very real problem in that society. It still means we should basically have one application of the law for all the people in this country. When we say Indians must have greater rights and must share in the rights of citizens, then, of course, along with any rights come responsibilities, and one of the biggest problems Indians face in living with this liquor problem is the problem of not knowing how to handle liquor, as has often been said. Many times we felt sure, in making liquor available to Indians through
[Mr. Badanai.l
public sources, commissions and so forth, that we were doing right, but we did not seem to go along with providing the education to meet the problems that would arise from the abuse of liquor. This is a problem which does not face the Indians alone.
There are many in the white community who abuse liquor, and many of us who have dealt with the failings of our fellow men know we cannot single out any one ethnic group as being more afflicted than any other by this kind of problem. While we look askance at the excessive consumption of liquor by people of Indian background we might also look for the real cause which leads them to use liquor to excess. If we look at some of the problems which the Indian people face through lack of education and job opportunities, and failure to find a place of acceptance in this country of ours, sometimes, as the fellow says, we can understand why it is enough to drive them to drink. Perhaps this is what the Indians as a people are doing, because of the confusion they face in trying to find their rightful place in our country.
Maybe this is only one way of helping the Indians. Maybe this is only one way of making them feel that they rate with the rest of us and have the same freedom as you and I do to abuse liquor and waste money. We have this freedom. Why does not the Indian have it? We say: You must be more careful how you spend your dollars. But I do think we have other ways of helping them than by legislating against the use of liquor. You cannot really legislate conduct, nor can you legislate people's attitudes. Our problem really is to find ways by which we can help those with liquor problems to better themselves. I know that in my own home town the provincial jail for women has its population predominantly composed of liquor offenders, and the greater number of these are women of Indian origin. It certainly is a problem, when you think that many of these women have families from whom they are separated during the period of incarceration. Yet these institutions which have people for limited periods of time are not able under present arrangements to offer any real, solid help to people with this problem. I think that when we have a more responsible and more conscientious attitude toward the whole problem of alcoholism-and this is something we cannot legislate-we shall have taken a long step forward.
Reference was made to the liquor option by the mover of this motion. I was interested to learn from the parliamentary secretary that in so many cases the different bands have already elected to permit liquor on their reserves. But I have experience of people with

this problem on a reserve within my own constituency at Sandy Bay, where this is not the case, and where the nearest police magistrate feels it is working a real hardship and a real unfairness on the residents of the reserve. You have on the one hand the privilege and the freedom of Indians to purchase liquor from the local hotel or liquor commission, yet they are not permitted to take it back to the reserve. This forces them to go to the houses of friends and consume more than they can properly handle or, at any rate, to get rid of it before getting back to the reserve where they can be fined for having it in their possession. It is apparent from the behaviour of the persons who are intoxicated that they have imbibed too freely. The local constabulary certainly finds on the highways persons proceeding to their homes who have imbibed too freely because of this legality which prevents them having liquor in their own homes.
So here we have not only a problem of liquor to the individual who is excessive in the use of it, but also a public danger on the highways from people driving while under the influence of liquor. I feel that while, in many instances, people feel they should control the use of liquor by preventing its presence on the reserves, they are really adding to the difficulty and adding to the danger. I I do not want to speak at great length on this matter because, as I said, I support the bill and would like to see it referred to committee for further consideration. As I said at the beginning of my remarks, Mr. Speaker, I think that basically it is a question of education, of counselling and helping these people to understand how they should use liquor, rather than legislating and preventing its use at all. For these reasons I would support the motion.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING POSSESSION AND CONSUMPTION OF INTOXICANTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett) has proposed Bill No. C-6, to amend section 93 through 96A of the Indian Act by combining sections 93 and 94 and making them applicable only to Indians living on a reserve. In addition, sections 95 through 96A would be repealed and replaced by a new section, 94 which removes the necessity for a request by the lieutenant governor in council to the province in order that the governor in council may proclaim that these subparagraphs relating to the sale of liquor to an Indian outside a reserve and to an Indian who has intoxicants in his possession outside a reserve, shall be no longer in force.
I support that part of the hon. member's amendment in that I think if a band council could refer directly to the governor in council unnecessary delays could be avoided. Moreover the amended section 94 proposed in Bill
Indian Act
No. C-6 retains the right of the governor in council to make regulations respecting votes and referendums, and maintains the requirements outlined in section 96A, paragraphs 3 and 5, conditioning the issuance of a proclamation by the governor in council on a request by a band council and referendum of the band. This guarantees that the band has an option. It eliminates the necessity for a resolution being presented to the attorney general of the province in which the reserve is situated.
I spoke on this bill when it was introduced last session and I dealt with what I considered to be three major objections to it. I shall go through these objections again because I feel they are valid and I honestly believe that this bill is not a good bill. I think the hon. member for Portage-Neepawa (Mr. Enns) touched on two of the main objections to this bill. He mentioned that people living on the reserve located in his constituency have voted in favour of eliminating the two paragraphs of the Indian Act which forbid the sale of alcohol to Indians off the reserve. However, these Indians are still subject to the rules governing the possession of alcohol within the reserve. One reserve located in my constituency has not voted. There has been no local option. The result is that the Indians on the reserve located in my constituency, who are living within five or ten miles of downtown Montreal, are not permitted to buy alcohol even off the reserve, nor are they permitted to have alcohol in their possession on the reserve. It appears to me that this is completely archaic. Most of these men are working in the United States, where they have the right to consume alcohol anywhere at any time. When they come back across the border they find themselves subjected to this completely antique, outdated and ridiculous hangover from the 19th century.
As I said, Bill No. C-6 is, I think, a slight improvement on the present act. Although it may be more flexible than the present act, it is less flexible than what is needed in the context of 1963. We are all prepared to admit, I think, that the abuse of liquor increases in direct proportion to the number of restrictions which are placed upon its use. I do not remember, but I think many hon. members of this house will remember what happened during the period of prohibition in the United States. This truism is certainly no less applicable to our Canadian Indians than it was to the American public during the 1920's. There is no question that the Indian Act regulations governing liquor must be amended, as must other sections of the Indian Act, to keep abreast of the rapidly changing circumstances of the Canadian Indian. Although it

Indian Act
may be true that in certain northern areas of our provinces-X am excluding the Northwest Territories because they do not have any reserves up there

regulations as stringent as the present regulations are necessary, in the vast majority of the reserves situated in southern Canada the present liquor regulations contained in sections 93 to 96A of the Indian Act are completely archaic. I am hopeful that the government will in this session decide to alter the present liquor regulations applicable to Indians in a manner which will mean that Indians throughout Canada will be subject only to the liquor regulations of the province within which their reserve is situated.
In order that the transition from stringent regulations to the normal, existing provincial regulations should not result in excesses in northern areas where such regulations have heretofore been rigorously enforced, it is my opinion that the minister should be given discretion to maintain certain of the regulations in force with regard to specified reserves only with the approval of the local band council, or with regard to reserves where he is requested to do so by the local band council. I would submit to the hon. member for Comox-Alberni that this would permit the flexibility which is necessary and which his bill does not provide.
As I mentioned earlier, Bill No. C-6 preserves these anachronisms. I find it very difficult to conceive of any law in Canada which could be more anachronistic than the present liquor laws as they apply to the Caughnawaga Indian reserve. Bill No. C-6 would continue, in part, this unfairness to a section of our population. A good portion of the present Indian Act is an indignity to our Indian population. The Indian Act regulations concerning liquor most certainly, I think, head the list of those regulations which do nothing but place our Indian population in a second class citizen category.
It reaffirms, as do a number of regulations in the Indian Act, the theory that the Indian is not equal to his fellow Canadians because he does not possess the qualities of self-control and self-regulation which the remainder of our population possesses. This theory is not tenable. It is completely without foundation and it has encouraged in this group, as it would in any group to which such regulations were applied, the very excesses which they were designed to curb.
I think the hon. member for Portage-Neepawa (Mr. Enns) made the point that our whole attitude toward the so-called sin of alcohol and its consumption is wrong; that the basic causes behind alcoholism are to be found more in social conditions and the environment in which any individual is living

and brought up, rather than in any other fundamental genetic weakness which might, according to the earlier theory, be the cause of alcoholism in individuals. Certainly I am not one of those who would consider for a moment that the Indian population of this country has any genetic weakness which makes it more subject to the evils of alcohol; this is simply not so.
The third major objection which I raised the last time when speaking on the bill is this.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING POSSESSION AND CONSUMPTION OF INTOXICANTS
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question before he goes on to his further point. With reference to his statements about the preservation of the right of local option, and in line with the earlier remarks of the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Badanai) about preserving Indian reserves, would the hon. member not agree that unless and until there is some broad and fundamental reallocation of jurisdiction -in other words, as long as we have the present Indian Act-this parliament should preserve the right of the freedom of Indians from having imposed upon them, on their reserves, laws in the provincial jurisdiction to which they might not agree?

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING POSSESSION AND CONSUMPTION OF INTOXICANTS
speechtext:
My answer to that, Mr. Speaker, is that the Indian Act should be revised so that the remaining regulations would be there only to protect what special rights our Indian population has by treaty. They should be there only to protect their special rights. Any other regulation in the Indian Act which in any way allows even a hint that our Indian population is being treated as second class citizens should be eliminated. I hope this government will take steps in this session to eliminate these many regulations which, in one way or another, place Indians in this inferior category.
I am in full accord with the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Bamett) about the necessity for retaining reserves in Canada, especially in the southern areas of the country. Unless Indian reserves are maintained, Indian culture in Canada will disappear completely. I think everyone in this house would agree that in this country of ours diversity culturally is much better than the sameness which permeates our neighbour to the south. I think that the Indian culture of this country has a role to play in our future. I think we should do everything in our power to encourage our Indian population to retain that culture. I also think that the Indian reserves of this country can be, if not viable economic units supporting the local Indian

population, at least the cultural home of the various Indian tribes living across the country.
My third main objection to Bill No. C-6 is that a piecemeal approach to remedying this particular liquor problem is not what is needed today. A piecemeal approach to an amendment of the Indian Act is not going to work. I will give an example of this. At the same time as we make fundamental liquor changes in the act we should also make sure at the departmental level that municipal policing regulations are placed in the hands of the local population. I think the Indian liquor problem, if such a thing exists, can be handled and best solved by the Indians themselves. I feel there has been a lack of support here from within the department. It is possible for local reserves to establish their own police force, but there has been a lack of support by the department for any move in this direction. I feel that this is one way in which we can give our Indian population the feeling that they are playing an equal role in the Canada of 1964; but we should encourage them to set up their own police force, and I think this should be done at the same time as we make these very necessary changes in the liquor regulations.
May I call it six o'clock, Mr. Speaker.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the recess I was speaking about the main objections that we have to the bill in its present form. I think I might summarize these by quoting
Electoral Boundaries Commissions again from Hansard of November 26, 1963, when the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Dief-enbaker) put these words on record:
We feel that the appointment of 10 commissions is not the answer to the problem. There should be a national commission.
While the house was adjourned for the supper recess I had the opportunity of looking up the precise date on which the resolution was introduced in the house by the former government. It was on April 9, 1962. The resolution was introduced by the then prime minister, now the Leader of the Opposition and, as found on page 2645 of Hansard for that date, it was in this form;
That it is expedient to introduce a measure respecting the establishment of an electoral boundaries commission for the readjustment of representation in the House of Commons; to provide that certain members of the commission may be paid such per diem allowance as may be fixed by the governor in council; to provide for the payment of reasonable travelling and living expenses for the members of the commission; and to provide also that the commission may engage the services of such technical advisers and other staff, including a person to act as secretary to the commission, as it deems necessary.
Having had an opportunity to read the debate following the introduction of that resolution, I should not have been surprised but I was rather astonished to notice the extent to which the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill), who has introduced the resolution now before the house, went in support of the resolution introduced at that time. He said this, as found on page 2650 of Hansard for that date:
I may say at once that the principle underlying the proposal is completely acceptable to the official opposition in this house. It is not only acceptable, but a resolution to that effect was formally adopted by the national council of the Liberal party.
Later he read from the resolution adopted by the Liberal party in these terms:
The Liberal party believes that redistribution of membership in the House of Commons should be carried out by a non-partisan commission.
There is no suggestion of any commissions, plural, in that resolution. He went on to quote the position of the Liberal party in these words:
Until now, this has been done only in the province of Manitoba, where the commission was established by a Liberal government. Redistribution means redrawing the boundaries of constituencies according to population.
Then he went on to discuss the technical requirements after each decennial census. Again, as found on page 2650 the minister had this to say:
It seems to me that the commission cannot be expected to make its own rules. That is our responsibility here in parliament.

Electoral Boundaries Commissions
Again it seems to me that the minister has departed from that in the provisions of the bill.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman permit me to interrupt him to clarify that point? I had the thought then that rules would embrace what is in the bill itself, that is, rules as to how redistribution should take place, which are in the bill now before the house, not rules about whether they would sit in the morning or afternoon or things of that sort.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: I thank the minister for his explanation. It seems to me it would have been more timely when he made these remarks and was being so critical of the introduction of the resolution when he was in opposition. Nevertheless, I hope he recognizes the point I have already made concerning the making of rules and regulations by 10 separate commissions whereby the likelihood will be that you will have 10 separate sets of rules and regulations emanating from 10 separate commissions.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: I wonder whether I could ask the hon. member a question for clarification. He commended, I thought with approval, the provision in the bill introduced some time ago by his leader that the rules should be made by the governor in council. Is that what he would think would be more appropriate?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
The rules that would have been made, as I anticipated the legislation, would have had this result, that parliament when considering the establishment of a national commission would have also considered the rules that would have been applicable to the procedures followed by the commission when it was reviewing the redistribution problems in the various constituencies across Canada. In the light of discussion as to what those rules and regulations should have been, I would have supposed that any government as reasonable as the last government was would have taken into consideration those discussions in establishing the order in council rules and regulations. This is a common procedure, and in a good many cases I am not fully in accord with the governor in council making rules and regulations under legislation, as a matter of fact because, with the superimposition of the federal authority on the peculiar situation we have in the Yukon, some 65 per cent of the ordinances and laws there are the result of orders in council and the making of regulations behind closed doors. The minister went on to say, as found on page 2651 of Hansard for the same date:
It seems to me that another thing that must be prescribed in addition to the maximum and minimum are what geographical, what historical and

what other conditions the commission is to take account of, and what exceptional provisions are to be made.
I take it that he was referring there to whether the tolerance should be 20 per cent or one third.
They must not be left to do this thing capriciously or without rules; that is our responsibility here.
Again I think I am in accord with the proposition the minister expounded there but it does not seem to me that it is clearly spelled out in the legislation, certainly not the minima and maxima in terms of geographical, historical and other conditions that might affect the setting of boundaries, and redistribution in the various constituencies. Arising from that debate and the debate that followed on April 10, 1962 there were press interviews given by the minister, and press reports based on the debate. I have one report here from the Edmonton Journal of October 13, 1962, which is rather humorous. It is written by Don McGillivray of the press gallery, and it reads in part as follows: Douglas Fisher, one of the biggest members of the Commons who represents one of the biggest ridings in Canada, moved that redistribution of constituencies be handled by a commission independent of the House of Commons.
The amusing part of the article is this:
Liberal Jack Pickersgill, still smarting under an attack on the Liberal party by Mr. Fisher, said the Port Arthur member was a "sort of grassroots egg-head" who had "joined the Prime Minister in a witch hunt for bureaucrats".
I recall that this was at a time when a resolution concerning the setting up of a national commission was under study. The article goes on as follows:
But he said the commission proposed, not responsible to parliament, would be a group of "superbureaucrats".
It seems to me that the bill that is now before us, introduced by the minister, compounds this situation 10 times, so that we have 10 times the number of superbureaucrats described by the minister now being proposed as acceptable to the house.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: I think perhaps the hon. gentleman would like me to clear up that point. I was referring to people who would be appointed by the government of the day. I took exception to the government of the day appointing any of the commissioners, and I have not changed my opinion. I think the commissioners should be prescribed in some way or other by parliament, or appointed by officers prescribed by parliament, and that is what the present bill would do.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
Here again, sir, when the last government appointed anybody, the appointee was a bureaucrat or a superbureaucrat. Now,

however, when the minister is sitting on the treasury benches any appointment made by his government is a proper appointment.

speechtext: But none of these appointments would be made by the government; that is the point the hon. gentleman does not seem to grasp. Under this bill, no appointments would be made by the government at all, and that was precisely the thing to which I objected during the debate two or three years ago. I said that we were not going to transfer redistribution from parliament to the cabinet. I have never varied from that view, and it is for this reason that in this bill we have been very careful to have no appointments made by the government, but to have appointments made by parliament or officers of parliament.

speechtext:
We were doing precisely that in appointing the chief justice. This is a government measure, and the minister cannot get around the fact that any government bill is going to be passed because of the government's majority. Let there be no mistake; the government has a majority in consequence of the arrangement that exists between the Liberal and Social Credit parties in this house. Whatever you call it, this is still a government appointment.
I have a press clipping here from the Ottawa Citizen dated April 18, 1962, in which the minister who is now holding forth about this being a perfectly acceptable proposal, criticized the intention to appoint judges to the commission because this, he said, would tend to drag the courts into politics. None the less, he is saying to the house that what he is proposing now is a proper thing. No doubt what he said in 1962 is quite wrong and I suppose that he has had another change of heart in that regard.
On April 10, 1962, this minister was accusing the former prime minister of delaying redistribution, of holding back progress for two years. He is saying now, however, that even if this bill is passed by this May it will be the spring of 1966 before anything can be completed with regard to redistribution. The Ottawa Journal of April 10, 1962, also carried an account of the minister's remarks at that time when he said that the government's delay in introducing it-meaning redistribution-would mean that no redistribution of parliamentary seats was likely for another two years. Then, the article continues:
He added that redistribution must not be taken out of the Commons to be placed in the hands of the cabinet. The commission's report should be presented unchanged to the house in the form of a representation bill.
Both of these matters were in the legislation introduced by the former government. I continue to quote from the article:
Electoral Boundaries Commissions
We are certainly not going to approve any measure that sets up a commission comparable in any way to the board of broadcast governors. We have had enough of that kind of impartiality in the last few years.
These words sound rather strange coming from the mouth of the Minister of Transport, who was for some time responsible for the activities of the C.B.C., particularly in the light of the C.B.C. programming and its notable partiality to his own party.
There is another excerpt from an article appearing in the Montreal Gazette of December 12, 1961 in which the minister referred to a commission rather than ten separate commissions. He said at that time, as reported in the Gazette of that day:
Liberal party spokesman J. W. Pickersgill said yesterday the official opposition will support Prime Minister Diefenbaker's plan to have an independent commission-
No suggestion here of any plurality of commissions.
-redraw the federal electoral map on the basis of this year's census.
In the Calgary Albertan of December 14, 1961, we find the editor saying this:
It is therefore encouraging to note that Hon. J. W. Pickersgill of the Liberal party has voiced his approval of the Prime Minister's intention.

All of these things taken together, the statement by the present Minister of Transport when he was in opposition and the statement made by the present Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) which I quoted from the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix, in which he held out the hope to the electorate of Saskatchewan that the minimum number of seats held by that province would not fall below what it now holds if a Liberal government were in office, all go to show that they are not so lily white as they are now trying to paint themselves. Before the recess I called these statements dishonest, fraudulent and deceitful, and so they were. I was mildly taken to task by the Minister of Transport for doing this. When I go back over some of the words that were used in this house about the prime minister of that day, now the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Dief-enbaker) I find that the words I used were mild indeed. The words that were used by the present Prime Minister, then leader of the opposition and those who sat with him including the minister, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) and the then member for Laurier, now our high commissioner to Great Britain, are remarkable examples of the extent to which they went. I cite such words as, "incredible effrontery"; "gross"; "unpardonable deceit"; "jeered"; "lying and betraying"; "besmirching the good
