Electoral Boundaries Commissions name of Canada"; "greater deceit"; "absolute rubbish"; "sneered"; "original as it is false". These are just a few examples of the terms that were applied to the prime minister of that day in what amounted to a complete disregard by those members who now sit over there of the dignity of the office of the prime minister. I say, sir, that when I described the words of the present Prime Minister and those who sit with him on the treasury benches as being deceitful, in the light of what they are trying to ask parliament to believe now, I am certainly not overstating the case.
Suffice to say that this measure is substantially the same measure that was introduced in April, 1962, by the Leader of the Opposition. There are three material defects in the legislation which I would hope could be changed by common agreement before the bill reaches the committee stage. The first is that the 20 per cent tolerance should be increased to a third, and I hope we shall find support from our friends to the left for that proposition. The second is that ten commissions, one for each province, will unnecessarily complicate and delay the work of redistribution. There should be one commission. There should be one commission predominated by judicial appointments.
When the Conservative party was in power it was suggested that these appointments should come from the Supreme Court of Canada and other judicial bodies. The fact remains that one commission can do the work in very much less time than can 10. I also think that a very strong argument in support of the one commission theory is the fact that 10 commissions, making 10 different sets of rules and regulations governing the procedures of their sittings, will contribute to chaos rather than uniformity of considerations applied to redistribution, despite the co-ordination by Mr. Castonguay, with all his excellent experience and knowledge being applied in that regard.
His running around to all these commissions, guiding them, giving them explanations and assisting them in the preparation of their work will be like a drop of water on a hot griddle, and it will take longer than one year to complete the work if the 10 commission theory is held to prevail. A further thought is that in making the rules and regulations, my personal view is that these should be submitted to the scrutiny of the parliamentary standing committee on privileges and elections, or that they should be discussed and some common agreement reached by all parties before the setting up of the commission.
Having set them forth, I would urge that the minister and the government take into

consideration these three proposals from this side, in the hope that we can reach an allparty agreement before the committee stage, and so expedite the passage of this very important legislation.

Mr. Speaker, I propose to base my opening remarks on the legislation that is now before us and not on the tenor of the last speech. I recall with interest the fact that when we were debating a companion bill on November 26 last I at that time, as today, had the opportunity of being the third speaker. The first one was the then secretary of state, now the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill). The second was the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker), and at that time I was in a position to say I felt in that debate we were demonstrating that the greatness of parliament is not only something of the past, but that it is something we can portray today.
I still feel, in what we are doing in this piece of legislation, that we are having an opportunity of redeeming parliament. In my view one of the blots on the Canadian parliament is the way in which redistribution has been handled throughout the decades of our history. I have had the personal experience of going through it twice. I was a member of the committees that sat in the 'forties and in the 'fifties and, as have other hon. members, I have read Hansard and Canadian history.
The way in which distribution has been carried out in the past is a sorry story. Therefore I think it is a high point in Canadian history when we have reached the position that all parties in the house agree this job should be done, not by members of parliament, as though they had a proprietary interest in their constituencies, but by an independent body or bodies of people outside parliament, on the basis of rules laid down by parliament in a public statute.
So far as the principle of this legislation is concerned, I regard it not just as good, not just as something we in this party are prepared to approve, but as a high point in

Canadian parliamentary history, and I hope that the debate as it proceeds will reflect the significance of what we are doing.
There never was any justification for the idea that sitting members of parliament should have the say over the drawing of the boundaries of the constituencies, and I am glad to note that the Conservative party, as long ago as 1903, 61 years ago, took a stand for the drawing of constituency boundaries by independent judicial bodies. But it does make one wonder why it was not done a long time ago. I chide the Liberals over the fact that it has taken them 45 years to carry out some of the things they pronounced in their 1919 platform; but the Tories tell us that for 61 years they have stood for redistribution by an independent commission. At least in two cases, when Sir Robert Borden was prime minister and when Mr. Bennett was prime minister, redistribution was in the hands of the Conservative party. I only wish they had done it then. It would have been better for Canadian history if they had.
However, we have reached the point now where the position taken by all parties is that the drawing of the boundaries of our constituencies is not the function of members of parliament, but that we should lay down the rules and then turn the job over to independent persons in whom we have the utmost confidence. Therefore I think we should look upon this bill not as a government bill-although by the nature of things it has to be-but as a bill that parliament is dealing with, as a bill that belongs to parliament, and we should do our best as members of parliament to make it the best bill that can possibly be drawn.
If we do that, if we come up with a bill that puts redistribution beyond partisan considerations, then we shall have done ourselves proud, but what is more important we shall have done a job of work for the parliament of Canada and for the people of this country.
The issues in this piece of legislation have been narrowed to two, three or four points. They have been referred to by the Minister of Transport and elaborated on by the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen). I think it is a good thing that we had some discussion of this matter in the last session of parliament, and for my part I wish to express my thanks to the Minister of Transport for the all-party consultation, without any commitments, that we had, so that we could narrow the field and get down to the things that we think should be discussed in connection with this bill. Therefore it is not my intention to take time even to comment on many of the things in the bill concerning which we are in agreement, but I do want
Electoral Boundaries Commissions to comment on some of the things about which there is disagreement, and I have one or two suggestions to make.
As a matter of fact, I want to tell the Minister of Transport that I accept his challenge on one point. He says he has racked his brains and could not find the answer. I accept his challenge when he suggests we should try to find a formula which would go right into this bill, and on the basis of which we could provide for the appointment of the commissioners in the bill itself rather than having two of them to be appointed, one by the Prime Minister and one by the Leader of the Opposition. Perhaps I had better deal with that point first, now that I have mentioned it. It had been my intention to deal, first of all, with the matter of there being 10 commissions proposed instead of one. However, since, when I get to that, I shall be arguing in favour of 10 commissions, we might deal first with the matter of how these commissioners are to be appointed.
The Minister of Transport says the reason we cannot, in this federal bill, follow the pattern of Manitoba by naming all the commissioners in terms of the offices they hold is that there are not comparable offices right across the country. You could, for example, in the four western provinces name the president of the provincial university but, as the Minister of Transport has pointed out, this would not be so easy in the case of provinces such as Ontario or Quebec. It has also been pointed out that there is no officer in each of the provinces holding a position comparable to that of chief electoral officer. It seems to me that the answer to this difficulty is quite simple. First, you could specify in the bill that the chairman of each commission shall be, as the bill now says, the chief justice of the province. I am sure that if there is any question about who is the chief justice in any province we could straighten that out. That is one appointee. The other appointee on which we all agree is the representation commissioner. What about the other two? I suggest we say that the other two should be as set out in the schedule to the act; and in the schedule which we could add to the act we could list the 10 provinces and we could decide here in parliament who are to be, by office, these other two commissioners, for British Columbia, Alberta, and so on. I would hope that in provinces where they have a provincial university one would be the president of that university and the other would be the chief electoral officer.
If there are provinces where there is no recognized provincial university, let parliament decide which university person or other officer we wish to put into that position. And

speechtext:
I will agree that the Minister of Transport may have raised a difficulty, but I suggest it is not beyond the wit of members of parliament to find an answer if we are agreed on the basic principle that we should be making the decision here in parliament, not leaving it to two individuals, particularly when each of those individuals has a party connection, to do a job which we are trying to put on a completely independent basis.
So I urge very strongly that consideration be given, when we get into committee on the bill, to making this kind of change with respect to the manner in which the members of the commissions are to be appointed.
This takes me to the second of the issues about which there has been debate, namely whether there should be 10 commissions or one. I say quite frankly to the hon. member who preceded me that I think he is involved in a good deal of hairsplitting when he quotes from speeches which have been made in the past and tries to find evidence of deception, dishonesty and all the rest of it in a change of position from one commission to 10. Surely, the principle is the same; the job is to be done by independent people outside of parliament, and surely there is not a great deal of difference between having one commission, but having it large enough that it can be divided into sections to do the job in the various provinces, and having ten commissions from the start, so that they can carry out the work which would have to be done in any case.
I submit that in addition to the time element to which the Minister of Transport

referred this afternoon there is also the inescapable fact that the people in any particular province know the situation in that province better than people removed from it. To take my own province, for example, it would be people like the president of the University of Manitoba, the chief justice of Manitoba and the chief electoral officer of Manitoba who would be most familiar with the general topography, the geography, the courses of the rivers and the lakes and all the rest of it, and who would be better qualified to judge the effect of changes and the drawing of boundaries than would one royal commission situated, shall we say, here in Ottawa and served, perhaps, by people who would not know very much about the situation in Manitoba.
I think these considerations apply right across the country. We want this job to be done in a manner which will appeal to the people as having been done fairly and honestly, and as having been done in the light of conditions in each part of the country I think we shall get a much better job if we have it done by people who belong to the province concerned and know the conditions in that particular province. I urge very strongly, therefore, that this house stay with the proposal in the bill that there should be 10 commissions to carry out this task of redistribution on an independent basis.
Now I move on to what I suppose will be the main controversial element in this whole piece of legislation-

Yes, numerically; in terms of population. Let us face the fact that in this legislation we are dealing mainly with the question of getting redistribution out of politics; of getting it done on an independent basis. But it is also a fact that we are, by virtue of some of the provisions of this bill, approaching in the direction of representation by population. Therefore if we are approaching in that direction, if that is one of the purposes of this bill, let us examine the question as to how well we are doing in that regard.
Hon. members know that section 51 of the British North America Act provides a number of interesting and complicated rules for the dividing up of the seats in the House of Commons among the various provinces. It is not done just on a proportional basis. The fact of the matter is, as we all know, that one seat is set aside for the Yukon Territory and that one seat is set aside for the Northwest Territories. We also know that we have the so-called senatorial floor and that in practice this will apply to any redistribution that now takes place in the provinces of Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick. There are four instances right
764	HOUSE OF
Electoral Boundaries Commissions there, Yukon, Northwest Territories, Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick, where a fixed number of seats will be determined by the rules in section 51 of the constitution. As a result those areas will all get greater representation than they would if redistribution were done on a strict population basis.
There is another interesting rule in the constitution. I call it affectionately the "Jimmy Gardiner rule". It was put in during the 1950's when the late Hon. James G. Gardiner was minister of agriculture. His aim was to find a way in which to save Saskatchewan from losing too many seats in the last redistribution. It did the trick for Saskatchewan in that redistribution. The rule is still there. It will not help Saskatchewan this time, but it does help Nova Scotia. This time Nova Scotia will, under the "Jimmy Gardiner rule", be saved one seat. Instead of dropping from 12 to 10, it will drop only from 12 to 11. That means you have Yukon, Northwest Territories, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia all with more seats than they would be entitled to on the strict basis of population.
I am not complaining about this; I am just setting out the facts. Therefore it is only the rest of the provinces, Newfoundland and the provinces from Quebec west, that are on a proportional basis; but it is only in relation to each other that they are on a proportional basis. The result is that you get a wide disparity in the quotient per province or per unit in this country. I have worked out a table that shows this, and I would like, Mr. Speaker, to have the consent of the house to place it on the record rather than boring hon. members with the figures. Let me tell the house what it is. I have entitled it "Anticipated redistribution of House of Commons electoral districts on basis of 1961 census and according to rules provided in section 51 of the British North America Act". In the first column I list the provinces, including the Yukon and Northwest Territories; in the second column I list the total population in 1961. This was according to the 1961 census. Then in the third column I list the number of constituencies that each province will get in the light of all these rules I have named. In the last column I list the average population per constituency.
The first column, of course, is simply a list of the provinces and the territories of Canada. The second column contains the actual population of these units according to the census of 1961. The third column contains the number of members assigned to each province or territory by the rules of the act. The total under the rules comes this time to 264. All that column amounts to is a dividing of the number of seats into the population, so that we arrive at the average in each case. Hon. members will notice the discrepancies that now exist. Supposing the 20 per cent tolerance holds-and I hope it does; in fact, I think it is too much already-and supposing the commissioners in one or more of the provinces take full advantage of that tolerance and make some seats 20 per cent more and other seats 20 per cent less than the actual quotient, what would be the result? New Brunswick's quotient being 59,793 it would be possible, even under this 20 per cent tolerance, for there to be a seat in Manitoba with a high of 85,077 and at the same time for there to be a seat in New Brunswick with a population as low as 47,835. That shows a disparity all the way from 85,000 to 47,000, and that is possible under the 20 per cent tolerance which now exists.
If the one third tolerance which the last hon. member who spoke argued for, were provided, it would be possible for one of Manitoba's seats to have 94,530 and another seat to have exactly half that, or 47,265. Here again, if I may compare a possible high in Manitoba with a possible low in New Brunswick you would go all the way from 94,530 for a seat in Manitoba to 39,862 for a seat in New Brunswick. Electoral Boundaries Commissions considered them but that we should not depart as far as we are being asked to from the principle that we represent people in this House of Commons and should therefore move in the direction of representation by population. Someone over there says that it should be down to 10 per cent. I agree, and if we bring it down 10 per cent we are still ending up with a ratio within a province 110 to 90. But we must remember that we have to consider these tolerances as superimposed upon disparities already existing. That is the reason that I asked permission to put my table on Hansard so that hon. members can look at the figures squarely and see the figures that already exist, and that the tolerances which are built on top of them compound the disparities.
Another matter which people are conscious of is this. Let me take, for example, the constituency of the Minister of Forestry (Mr. Sauve) at the present time. He represents 10,000 or 12,000 good Canadians, whereas the hon. member for York-Scarborough (Mr. Moreau) represents several hundred thousand of them. That is the sort of disparity we want to avoid. We represent people, and every individual's vote should have some kind of equal weight in this House of Commons. We will not have that even with this bill; we will still have wide discrepancies. And in all this I have left out any reference to the extreme case of only 26,000 in each of the constituencies of Prince Edward Island-and if a tolerance of 20 per cent is applied that figure could be even lower.
I have not complained about the small population in the north. It is provided in the British North America Act that we agree that those areas should have special representation. But having gone that far let us not compound the problem or make it worse or keep our representation completely out of line with population, as would be the case if we made the tolerance any greater.

Yes, Cariboo too. But the point I want to make, and I was given a bit of a cue by the 10 per cent interjection from across the way, is that I think the commissioners, when they are set up and are ready to study this matter, will be aware of what has been done in countries like Australia and New Zealand, where when they have a maximum tolerance up or down the commissioners do not start out with that maximum tolerance, but only use about half of it. They reserve the maximum tolerance up for unusual situations or the maximum tolerance down for the very sparsely settled ridings, areas such as the ridings in this country of Port Arthur, Cariboo, Churchill, Bonavista-Twillingate, Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador, and so on. I hope that that will be the case here, that the commissioners will not start by saying they can go 20 per cent up for all the urban ridings and 20 per cent down for all the rural ridings, but that they will lay down some principles about population per square mile which will cover the situation of these far northern ridings and try to keep the tolerance down to 10 per cent, so that we get closer to representation by population than has yet been the case.
Therefore, I say that there should be a really serious study of these figures I have put on the record, particularly those in the fourth column of the table. I also ask hon. members before they make proposals for larger tolerances to do the arithmetic on these figures and see how wide the discrepancy can be between constituencies with low populations in New Brunswick, Newfoundland or Nova Scotia and constituencies with high populations in Ontario, Manitoba or the western provinces. After all, it is still a basic fact that what we represent in the House of Commons is people, not square miles or stones and trees but Canadian people, and we should move as far as we can in the direction of that kind of representation.

Let us not kid ourselves. We do not contact every person in our ridings, whether we are in a rural area or in an urban area. Having got that feel and having tried to do the job I submit that the situation should not be as it is now, where 75,000 people in Winnipeg North Centre have one member to represent them and 10,000 people in Iles-de-la-Madeleine have also one member to represent them. Or perhaps I should give the comparison between the hon. member for Iles-de-la-Madeleine (Mr. Sauve) and the hon. member for York-Scarborough.
In this piece of legislation, under the terms of the bill itself, we are dealing with two main matters. One is that of taking redistribution out of politics, which the bill does and does very well. The other point that we are dealing with under the terms of the bill, because of this idea of a quotient and not departing by more than a certain tolerance, is an attempt to move in the direction of representation by population.
But if we put the tolerance too high we will completely destroy any effort we are making to move in that direction. So I hope, Mr. Speaker, that when we get into committee on this bill and go through it clause by clause there will not be any acceptance by

the house of any proposal to widen that tolerance. I would hope that instead the house might go the other way and reduce it to 15 per cent or even less.
I also hope, Mr. Speaker, that we will stand by the 10 commissions, but on the matter of the appointment of these commissions I strongly urge that we use our wits-despite the fact that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) sees some difficulty I think it can be got over-to find a way whereby we can name these people in the bill that goes through parliament by their offices, and not leave it so that two of the people are going to be appointed by two of the party leaders of this country.
There is just one other thing I want to say about the bill, and there has not been very much comment about this section yet. I am glad the bill embodies the principle that if an outside, independent body is going to do the job it should not then be our right here in parliament to alter, to amend, to have the say whether it goes through or not. I think the proposal that when the commissioners make their report it can be discussed in parliament in terms of detail only if one third of the members in any province file a motion to that effect is a happy thought. I was not happy about previous proposals for redistribution that implied that after an independent body had done the job parliament could do it all over again. I suppose this is partly because I have been through two of these redistribution experiences. They are not parliament at its best and I do not want to see that situation brought back in any way whatsoever. Therefore I am glad that those who drafted the bill have given parliament the chance-it is not the government's bill; it is parliament's bill-really to go all the way, so that this business of drawing the boundaries of constituencies for the people of Canada will not be done by those who have a vested interest such as we have here, but by an independent body.
As I say, Mr. Speaker, we welcome this bill. We think there are one or two improvements that could be made. We think that the business of having 10 commissions is a more expeditious way to deal with the matter and we think that the tolerance should not be large. If anything, it should be less than 20 per cent now proposed so that as far as possible we will do two jobs, first, take redistribution out of politics and, second, move in the direction of representation by population. I urge this on the basis of the fact that our job here is to represent the people of Canada as people.

speechtext:
The hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) says that I should not be quite so sanctimonious. May I suggest that there are a number of members of his party who have evidenced quite a bit of the same spirit in days gone by.
The principle of the measure before us at the present time is one that commends itself to the members of the house. It was introduced first on December 20, 1963, which has allowed sufficient time for many people to express their views publicly with regard to the matter. Even if the suggestions made have been widely varied, I believe there is general agreement on the principle that there should be an independent body or bodies established to carry out the important and necessary task of redistribution.
This is the second measure required to facilitate the redrawing of the electoral boundaries on the basis of the 1961 census and, of course, to carry out the subsequent redistributions as they are required. First of all we were called upon to consider a measure to establish the office of representation commissioner. That gave us an opportunity

Electoral Boundaries Commissions to debate not only that particular issue but also many other factors in relation to the whole problem of redistribution.
If it is necessary to state the position of the Social Credit party in this connection once again, I should like to assure the house that we are in full support of the principle of the bill and will co-operate in its passage. As I indicated, I had the opportunity of participating in debate on this subject some weeks ago and my remarks are found on pages 5136 and 5137 of Hansard for November 26, 1963. Many of the statements I made at that time set forth principles and convictions that we still have in regard to the measure now before us.
The project of redrawing the electoral boundaries in Canada is a very important and highly necessary one. It is necessary from the constitutional standpoint, but practical considerations make it essential that this matter be dealt with from time to time in order that the people of Canada may be better served through the electoral machinery that has been established by parliament. On different occasions the various factors involved have been brought to the attention of the house. One thinks of the increase in the population of our country, which is now over 19 million, and along with the increase there has been a shifting in population. Immigration policies have also played a part in the increase in population, and we find that there has been a tendency for the population to diminish in some places and increase in others. This brings the fact to our attention that redistribution is essential in order to maintain a semblance of balance, as far as representation in the house is concerned.
Having recognized that fact, I am sure it is the desire of every member of the house to discover the fairest possible way in which redistribution can be brought about, having regard to all the legitimate factors involved. The measure before us, as has been pointed out, calls for the setting up of 10 commissions. Perhaps this is not the important issue before us. Nevertheless, it does constitute a very important part and one which I am sure will require considerable attention.
I should like to refer to the urgency of this matter. The last census was taken in 1961 and, of course, we are now well into 1964. This means that a good part of the 10 year period has already elapsed since the last census. I believe that the work of redistribution should be facilitated. I believe that it should be commenced as soon as possible and carried through just as expeditiously as possible in order that before another election is called we can proceed on the basis of the redistribution. I think that this adds to the

sense of urgency in connection with the work that is before us at the present time.
I should like to refer, sir, to a number of the considerations involved that have been mentioned by other members participating in the debate. A question has been raised in connection with how many commissions we should have. How many commissions are necessary in order to carry out this project in the shortest possible time and yet in the fairest possible way? We have one suggestion that there should be one commission established whose responsibility it would be to carry out redistribution in every part of Canada from coast to coast. Another suggestion is that we should divide the country into areas, possibly four areas, with a commission responsible for each of them.
In this connection, I should like to point out one of the problems involved. Consider for a moment the wide variations that exist between conditions in the province of Saskatchewan, for instance, and the province of British Columbia and we will see how difficult the job would be. In Saskatchewan, they have the prairies and they do not have any of those great natural barriers that we have in British Columbia. Of course, the problems would not be as pronounced there as they are in British Columbia.
Then, we have the suggestion contained in the bill before us, namely that we should have a commission for each province. I suggest that one commission for each province would or should result in a more satisfactory redrawing of the electoral boundaries having regard to all the relevant factors. So far as we in this group are concerned, therefore, we would prefer to see the suggestion in the bill maintained and have one commission for each province. The question, however, of the appointment of the commissioners is something that should be considered. A statement has been made on numerous occasions that the desire is to eliminate political considerations. I feel this is commendable. I have not had too much to do with redistribution in years gone by, but there have been references to political pressures, political considerations, that have entered into the redrawing of the electoral boundaries. I would not know anything about that. However, I do recognize the fact that those who have been here the longest seem to be the strongest advocates to have redistribution taken out of the political arena and handed over to an independent body.
Having said that, and having pointed this out, we find that the provisions in the bill indicate two politicians are to be called upon to appoint some of the commissioners. I use the term "politicians" in the best sense of the word. I am not casting any aspersions, I am

just referring to the fact that these two right hon. gentlemen are in the political field. They are the heads of political parties and, therefore, it seems to me that we are not departing far enough from the principle that was enunciated. We ought to find some other way of making these appointments.
In considering this particular matter, we would like to suggest that these commissions could be made up, for instance, of the representation commissioner, the chief justice of the province concerned and the provincial chief electoral officer. I know that in discussing this matter the minister has called attention to the problems involved. I do not believe those problems are insurmountable. If the problems had been insurmountable, perhaps this would have been ascertained in Australia.
I should like to refer to an editorial which appeared in the Gazette of January 3, 1963, and I shall read one paragraph:
In each of the six Australian states, the federal government appoints three electoral commissioners to investigate these population changes. The commissioners are public servants, and usually comprise the chief electoral officer of the state concerned, the head of the land survey section in the state concerned, and a third person with similar qualifications.
Now, to those who will make reference to the objection to appointing the chief electoral officer because of the problems involved,
I should like to point out that in Australia the state electoral officers are members of the commission. It does not seem, therefore, as though Australia found any insurmountable obstacles as these commissions were formed. We would suggest that the provincial chief electoral officers would be the men who would be eminently qualified to deal with this important matter. They are aware of the problems. They are aware of the geographical problems, the population trends, and all of these other factors that must be taken into consideration. If anyone should know about these factors and understand them, I would suggest the chief electoral officer is the one best qualified to give consideration to these matters. We would suggest that this idea be given careful consideration.
In introducing this measure, the Minister of Transport stated that having the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition make the appointments we would be assured of impartiality. I just do not believe this. I think the reasons are obvious. Appointments by these two right hon. gentlemen would not necessarily assure impartiality. If we are going to get away from political considerations, political elements, let us get away from them and do what we want to do. We should place these appointments in the hands of those who are not connected with or in
10,	1964
Electoral Boundaries Commissions position of leadership of political parties. Let us have truly independent individuals, independent commissions.
I should like to mention some of those factors that must be considered in redrawing electoral boundaries. The other day, speaking in the debate, my colleague from the Cariboo mentioned three things that were vitally important; population, topography and geography. I would refer the house to some of the statements my colleague made on that occasion because I think they are very important, not only in relation to the issues under discussion then, but to the discussion which we are having today.
I would like to refer again to the editorial in the Montreal Gazette of June 3, 1963, and read another paragraph which is as follows:
The commissioners are required to divide the 5,000,000 Australian voters into 122 electorates, which average between 40,000 and 50,000 voters each, and base their decisions on community of interest, transport facilities, and natural boundaries, such as rivers and mountain ranges.
This brings in the same thought as my colleague referred to the other day, and I believe these matters should be taken into consideration in the redrawing of the electoral boundaries.
There has been considerable discussion tonight, some of it good-natured, regarding the principle of representation by population. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) stated that we were representing people, not stones and trees. We may possibly agree with that. We are representing people; but we must remember that the people should have access to their elected representatives, and if they are to do that, then widespread areas should be given special attention. Therefore, even though the principle of representation by population may sound pretty good, there are many other factors which have to be taken into consideration in the over-all picture.
There is just one other matter which I would like to mention, and that is the tolerance percentage stipulated in the bill. It is set at 20 per cent, and there are hon. members who believe that this is far too low. I was almost going to use the terms, conservative and liberal, but I do not like those terms. There are others who think it is far too high. Personally I would be inclined to say it is a pretty good compromise between those two positions, and when we consider the effect of this 20 per cent tolerance applied to various constituencies, I do not believe we can get anything closer to the needs of the facts as they are presented and recognized by all of us.
I believe in some places the degree of tolerance is set at 5 per cent. That might be

Electoral Boundaries Commissions a little too rigid and, as I have said, I think the 20 per cent tolerance is a fairly good compromise between the positions of those who think it should be higher and those who think it should be lower. While adjustments may have to be made, and at times are made in the light of experience, I believe this legislation will result in a far more efficient and effective redrawing of electoral boundaries than was the case in the past.
We request that the government give consideration to the composition of the commissioners as we have outlined tonight. We think that if this suggestion were incorporated in the bill it would help to achieve what we desire, the elimination of party consideration so far as that is humanly possible.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as did hon. members who preceded me, I take pleasure in participating in this discussion on Bill C-72, concerning the setting up of commissions to be established in the provinces to study the boundaries of the various ridings.
Since the 1961 census, everybody has been able to see that the counties have changed. Therefore, this bill provides for a redistribution by population rather than by acreage. When looking at the results of the 1961 census, we find that the population in certain rural ridings has decreased to the benefit of the cities, and that some districts also lost part of their population to the benefit of other districts.
This bill aims at correcting anomalies resulting from the increase or decrease of population in some districts.
In discussing this bill we have to settle two questions; first of all whether each province should have a commission and second, whether a minimum of 20 per cent or more should be considered.
In respect of the first point, and as the minister asked us for suggestions to help him prepare a bill which would be the best answer to the needs of the various ridings in Canada, I suggest that four commissions would do an adequate job. For instance, one commission might look after the western provinces, comprising 70 ridings. I suppose that it would be possible to find in the four western provinces-Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia-somebody who would be really familiar with the problems of the constituencies concerned, as well as with all the mountains, rivers and topographical characteristics. Ontario could also have its commission, for, with 85 constituencies, it is quite an important province. The same applies to the province of Quebec, which has 75 constituencies. As concerns the maritime provinces, I believe it would be stupid to

establish a commission for a province with less than 10 constituencies. In my opinion, one commission could certainly meet the requirements of the 35 constituencies or so of the maritime provinces, the Northwest Territories and the Yukon.
They have intelligent people in the maritime provinces and it would be easy to find capable persons to settle problems to the satisfaction of these four provinces.
This would first of all prevent centralization, as suggested by the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) who wanted a single commission to settle the problems throughout Canada. On the other hand, this could prevent confusion or delays in decisions to be made concerning the boundaries of the constituencies concerned.
We therefore think four commissions, that is one for the western provinces, one for Ontario, one for Quebec and one for the maritime provinces, would very well meet the needs or redistribution.
As mentioned by the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Patterson), this bill, under section 6, leaves to two politicians-let us grant they have good intentions-the appointment of two members on these commissions. So, two men interested in politics are asked to appoint two members, no account being taken of other political ideologies presently existing in Canada. It is proposed to set up independent commissions, but those two men are entrusted with the task of appointing the commissioners for each province.
The formula I would suggest would be much more democratic. In my opinion, consideration should be given to the result of the vote in each province. Let us see what it was for the last election. Would it be proper for the Liberal party to appoint a commissioner in Alberta when they got fewer votes than the Social Credit party?
I would say that, in Alberta, the leader of the official opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) and the Social Credit party should each appoint a commissioner.
On the other hand, in British Columbia, the present Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) could appoint one commissioner since the Liberals got the majority of votes and the New Democratic party could appoint the other commissioner since its candidates were ahead of the Social Credit candidates. As for the Conservatives, I do not see why the present leader of the official opposition, should choose a commissioner in that province.
Different problems face other provinces, and the different results must be taken into consideration.
For instance, in the province of Quebec, people wonder why the leader of the official opposition should appoint a commissioner

when the Conservative candidates got less votes than the Social Credit candidates. Consequently, it seems to me that, in the province of Quebec, the present Prime Minister should appoint one commissioner and the leader of the group that got the next highest percentage of votes should appoint one also. Such being the case, as far as the province of Quebec is concerned, the Prime Minister would select one commissioner and the leader of the Ralliement Creditistes, the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette), the other one.
When we consider the results of the 1963 election, both from a democratic and a percentage standpoint, we find that what is proposed on page 2 of the bill now before us is contrary to the idea of setting up an independent commission.
If we want to follow democratic principles and respect the opinion of all members, I feel we should proceed in the manner that I have just suggested. That would allow all political party leaders equally to select a commissioner in one or the other of the different Canadian provinces.
The leader of the New Democratic party would then appoint a commissioner in British Columbia; the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Thompson) would appoint one in Alberta; the hon. member for Villeneuve would pick one for the province of Quebec. And the present leader of the government, as well as the present leader of the official opposition, would select the commissioners in the other provinces.
This would be a true reflection of the situation in the house according to the people's choice in the last election. In short, the percentage of votes in each province could be used as a basic principle. Then everybody would be satisfied and nobody could complain of frustration.
When carrying out a bill such as this one which is of such prime importance for the future of the members, we must at once lay solid foundations so as not to regret, later on, injustice towards anyone.
Coming back to the suggestion made in this bill with the phrase "20 per cent more or less", I think that for the time being it is a sensible suggestion because if we have to make changes and redistribute the electoral districts on the basis of their population, we shall have to proceed very intelligently for the reason that should we realize, within a few years, that the rural centres are losing even more of their people to the urban centres, we would have to amend the act once more.
All the more so since one of the most difficult things in rural ridings is to reach
Electoral Boundaries Commissions all the people because it takes much more time and it costs a lot.
I feel that the standard set in this bill, that is "20 per cent more or less" is a sound one. We have nothing else to suggest, except keep the debate free from political partisanship.
In closing, I point out that it would be useless to set up a commission in the provinces which have only four members or fewer than 10.
For instance, I think that one commission might very well be able to carry out the duties mentioned in this bill, and in the case of the maritime provinces, receive the representations that people might make in order to amend or correct the number or limits of electoral districts.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
I must say at once that I am in full agreement with the principle of a non-partisan commission to redistribute electoral boundaries in Canada.
There are a number of principles contained in this particular bill to which reference has been made. The first concerns the question of whether there should be one commission or 10 commissions. My own view is, and has been, that one commission would be preferable. This has been our stand throughout. However, there has already been a great deal of discussion on this particular point. I wish to deal with two other matters. One of them has been touched upon already, and the other has not.
The first concerns the 20 per cent clause. I wish to say immediately that I disagree completely with the views of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) in this regard. Perhaps there is a difference between us because I represent a rural riding whereas the hon. member represents an urban one, and I suppose each of us is inclined to believe he has a tougher job to carry out than have the other members of this house. To this extent I defer to the hon. member's personal opinion. But it is my belief that a 20 per cent tolerance in connection with population is far too low. This is based on my submission that members representing rural ridings have not only a great deal more territory to cover but a great many more duties to perform than have urban members.
Let us consider the huge ridings, geographically speaking, of which we have a number in Canada. It would seem to me that efforts should be made to reduce the area of some of these enormous ridings-I think of Meadow Lake and Mackenzie in Saskatchewan, and various others in northern Ontario, for example, which are much too large for one

Electoral Boundaries Commissions member to cover adequately. But if we apply the 20 per cent tolerance formula to these ridings it becomes obvious that a number of them will have to be made larger still, rather than smaller, and that some of these huge areas, representing something like a quarter of the area of a whole province, would be increased still further to something approaching one third. I believe that in cases such as these the way should be open for a reduction of these huge ridings which it is almost impossible for a single member to represent adequately. Instead, their area is increased rather than diminished.
I should like to mention, too, the average rural riding. I believe the member representing a rural riding is called upon to give more service per capita to his constituents than is the member representing an urban riding. I do not wish to detract in any way from the work done by members who represent a large number of constituents. I am merely saying that in rural areas where there are small pockets of population and large numbers of small communities, largely separate, the rural member has a good deal more work to do. In addition, he is in closer contact, I believe, with the people who live in these communities. I believe the people in these smaller units have more reason to contact their members of parliament than is the case in urban areas. I think, too, that rural members have more duties in connection with such matters as post offices, wharves, docks, agricultural problems, municipal affairs, and so on, probably as a result of a closer association with the people whom he serves.
To illustrate this I would point out that in an urban area an individual who may have a problem which does not relate strictly to the federal duties of a member can go to municipal authorities, to the local branches or offices of provincial departments, and find the person who is prepared to deal with his problem. The situation is the same in the federal field; in a large urban area there is an office of the unemployment insurance commission, the national employment service, the civil service commission, the Department of Public Works, and so forth. In the smaller communities these people are not available. In many of the rural ridings there are no representatives of federal departments. As a result, instead of being able to go to the local offices of the department, residents are required to go to their member of parliament for assistance. In many cases this could be eliminated very easily by a routine inquiry at an office. I say this for the reason that there is required a greater service per capita. In the urban and the central areas the government, at government expense, sets up the district offices for all its departments, and the


people living within that community or city can go to those offices and have their questions answered and their problems given some attention. In the rural areas we have to handle these things ourselves, and I do believe it makes a good deal more work for the member.
I believe, also, that in a rural area there are more contacts with municipal officials. Here again, in a great many cases they are not strictly federal matters, but if there is no one else to go to, I think it is the experience of us all that people go to the person who has been most recently a subject of public attention. The fact that we have had four elections in the last six years has meant that the member of the federal parliament, or candidate for election, has received more publicity, and it is a fact that as elections approach people are inclined to write to the person whose name they see before them. In this way, therefore, we do have these additional problems.
There is another question, Mr. Speaker. While population is important, we cannot overlook the fact of Canadian geography. The national objective of this country is, I believe, that of the expansion and development of underdeveloped areas. If we provide insufficient members of parliament to service these huge areas which are about to be developed, we are not thereby promoting the attention to development that might otherwise be the case. If we give representation of a large area to one member, we are giving an impossible job to a person who might otherwise be looking after expansion and development in a better manner. It is a fact of Canadian geography that we have these tremendously large areas. These members may not represent a great many people now, but they will represent a great many people in the future. These areas do require members to be here in this house to put forward proposals for development, and to keep the attention of the government focused on the fact that this large area has potential, which otherwise might be overlooked.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I do not think it is right to say that in Canada representation by strict population is fair either to the people or to the country. This may be the case in other areas which are well settled or which are more or less evenly settled, but at this stage of our development in Canada I do not think it is fair and proper to take the larger areas and to them only assign one member because there are not very many people living in the area.
I should like to refer to some actual figures for a moment to illustrate the point I am trying to make. I was very appreciative of the

table put before the house by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). I also obtained some figures which are very close to his on this particular matter. I should like to take the province of Ontario as an example, based on the most likely redistribution, with an average population of about 70,000 persons per riding. Taking the 20 per cent variance that is now provided in the bill, only 31 of the present 85 seats would come within this 20 per cent. That is, only 31 of the 85 would not have their boundaries altered. If we increased the variance to 33J per cent, or one third, an additional 23 ridings would be undisturbed by redistribution. But in addition to this there are another 31 ridings which, whether the variance is 20 per cent or 33J per cent, are bound to have their boundaries changed because they have a very small population or a very large one.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that the objective of redistribution is to give improved representation to the people and to make the representation of each individual more equal in this house. I think it should also be an objective that as few as possible traditional voting patterns and voting areas should be disturbed. On this basis I would say that if we could, by accepting a one third tolerance, give fair and equal distribution without disturbing traditional voting patterns, it would be much more fair. For this one province even, with a variance of 33J per cent there would still be 31 Ontario ridings which would have to be changed, and this must automatically affect to some degree the adjacent ridings. For those reasons, Mr. Speaker, I believe that a 20 per cent tolerance in a country such as Canada is not sufficient and we should raise it, to be fair, to at least a one third tolerance.
My second objection concerns the procedure to be followed in giving effect to the report of the commissioners. As is set out in the bill which we have before us, the procedure is something like this. The commissioners for the province give their report and it is transmitted to Mr. Speaker and tabled here in the house. Following that, if there is objection to the report one third of the members from any given province may give formal notice. If that objection is raised by signed petition, the matter can be brought to a vote of the house. We will suppose there is an objection by one third of the members and that the house, by vote, decides that the commission has made a mistake and the boundaries are not right. Therefore a resolution is passed referring back to the commission the report which they made. The commission can then ignore completely the vote which was taken in the House of Commons by the majority of the members and 20220-50
Electoral Boundaries Commissions say: "Well, this may be parliament's opinion but it is not ours, and we confirm what we have already said". I say that this is a complete abrogation of the principle of the supremacy of parliament.
In this bill we are trying to take this matter out of political partisanship. Therefore, if we are going to do that we should not allow an intervention of parliament which can then be abrogated by an inferior body such as the commission. We must not be put in a position where parliament makes a decision and then says to the commission: "You have made a mistake in the boundaries which you have made out, so reconsider your report", and then have the commission saying: "Well, we do not agree with you". This is a situation which is not a correct one, and the bill should be amended before it is brought into effect.
I have a solution to this problem, Mr. Speaker-because there is no use in objecting unless you have one. If we are going to insist on the commission's having the last word, then I submit that it should not have the last word after parliament has made a decision. My proposal is that if there are objections raised in the house by a sufficient number of members from the province concerned the reports will then automatically go back to the commission instead of going back by a motion of the House of Commons. In this case the objections would have been met and satisfied, the attention of the commissioners drawn to the fact that members of the house are not satisfied with their report, and they can then reconsider the matter. But it should not be a formal act of the House of Commons to refer the matter back, because we are just making the House of Commons look ridiculous if the house makes a report one way and another body says they do not agree with it, that they stand by their original report. So to this extent I think the bill ought to be amended. It should be either one thing or the other. If parliament is to have the last say, then it should have it. If parliament is not going to have the last say, then let us not go through the formality of a vote in this house only to see it abrogated.
Frankly, I have always felt that parliament should have the last say in the question of an appeal. I still think this is a proper procedure, and I have always felt that the commission's report ought to be accepted unless the house, having voted on the matter, finds an error. The House of Commons should be the court of appeal in this matter, as it is in any other. I have not changed from this viewpoint because I think we have to accept the responsibility for our

On this same point, Mr. Speaker, I was interested to find that the bill provides that if one third of the members from any one province raise objection, action is then taken. Naturally, being interested in my own position in the house as a member of the Progressive Conservative party from the province of Ontario, I ask myself what it does to me. Well, Mr. Speaker, the Conservative party has 27 members from Ontario in this house out of a total of 85 from the province. We are just about four members short of being able to raise objection to the report which comes in. Here we are in the position that if we do not agree with the report brought in for the province of Ontario the members of the official opposition are unable to do anything about it, because we are just a few members short of one third. That is why I am suspicious of the fact that one third is suggested. I am going to suggest that one quarter is sufficient.
The members on the government side have two dandy alternatives. If they like the report they let it in. If they do not like the report they can appeal it. Unfortunately, we on this side of the house acting alone cannot do this, nor can any of our friends from the other parties, unless we all join together in one grand slam. Perhaps we will not agree. speechtext: Does he think that the proportion of members from a given province who can put down an objection is too high if it is one third?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: And that it should be, say, one quarter; or that any one member should be able to do it?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker, I do not go that far. I do no think that any one member should do this. I am suggesting that in the particular circumstances and in the light of the situation here, there is a provision in the bill as it now stands which appears to me to be partisan and unfair. It may not have been intended that way and I stand to be corrected by some of my colleagues; but whether it is intended or not, it is partisan and unfair. We represent a large number of members in a province which will have 89 or 90 seats in the house. Therefore I feel, under these particular facts and circumstances, that one third is too high, particularly if my suggestion is accepted that a substantial number of objections would be sufficient to have the report sent back without a formal vote of the house. I should like to suggest that one quarter shoud be the proportion, but that is purely for my own selfish reasons, I admit. Nevertheless, here is a situation which will leave certainly the Conservative members from Ontario in a very difficult position.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: Could the hon. gentleman say where it would leave the Liberal members from Saskatchewan?
